1: # Schedules
2: 
3: `tally/schedule.py` reads cron-style schedule expressions. Implement `matches(expr, when)`
4: and `next_run(expr, after)` exactly as described here. Times are naive `datetime` objects;
5: there are no time zones or daylight saving changes.
6: 
7: ## Expressions
8: 
9: An expression is five fields separated by one or more spaces or tabs. Leading and trailing
10: whitespace is ignored.
11: 
12: | Field | Values | Names |
13: |---|---|---|
14: | minute | 0-59 | |
15: | hour | 0-23 | |
16: | day of month | 1-31 | |
17: | month | 1-12 | `JAN`-`DEC` |
18: | day of week | 0-7, where 0 and 7 are both Sunday | `SUN`-`SAT` |
19: 
20: Names are the first three letters of the English month or day name, in any case. They are
21: only allowed in the month and day-of-week fields. Numbers are plain decimal digits; leading
22: zeros are fine.
23: 
24: Each field is a comma-separated list of one or more items. An item is one of:
25: 
26: - `*`: every value of the field.
27: - `N`: a single value.
28: - `A-B`: every value from A to B. If A is greater than B, the range wraps around: it counts up from A to the field's maximum, then carries on from the field's minimum up to B, so `22-2` in the hour field is 22, 23, 0, 1 and 2. In the day-of-week field a wrapping range counts through 0 to 6 with 7 treated as 0, so `FRI-MON` is Friday, Saturday, Sunday and Monday.
29: - Any of the above followed by `/S`, where S is a whole number of at least 1. Of the values
30:   the item lists, in order, it keeps the first and then every S-th one after it, so `*/15`
31:   in the minute field is 0, 15, 30 and 45. `N/S` lists N up to the field's maximum.
32: - Day of month only: `L`, the last day of the month.
33: - Day of week only: `NL`, the last day N of the month (`5L` is the last Friday), and `N#K`,
34:   the K-th day N of the month, where K is 1 to 5 (`1#2` is the second Monday). Here N is a
35:   number from 0 to 7, not a name.
36: 
37: A whole day-of-month or day-of-week field may also be `?`, which means the same as `*`.
38: 
39: Instead of five fields, an expression may be one of these shortcuts, in any case:
40: `@yearly` and `@annually` (`0 0 1 1 *`), `@monthly` (`0 0 1 * *`), `@weekly` (`0 0 * * 0`),
41: `@daily` and `@midnight` (`0 0 * * *`), and `@hourly` (`0 * * * *`).
42: 
43: Anything else raises `ValueError`: the wrong number of fields, a value outside its field's
44: range, an empty item, a step of 0, a name in the wrong field or in a step, `L`, `NL` or `N#K`
45: in the wrong field, a `?` outside the two day fields, an unknown shortcut, and so on. Both
46: functions check the whole expression first and raise `ValueError` for a bad one, whatever
47: the other argument is.
48: 
49: ## When a schedule runs
50: 
51: A schedule runs at every minute whose minute, hour and month are listed in their fields, on
52: every day that is allowed. A day is allowed only when it matches both the day-of-month field and the day-of-week field. A field that is `*` or `?` matches every day.
53: 
54: `matches(expr, when)` returns `True` if the schedule runs at `when`'s minute. Seconds and
55: microseconds are ignored.
56: 
57: `next_run(expr, after)` returns the first run strictly after `after`, as a `datetime` with
58: zero seconds and microseconds. For a schedule that runs every minute, both 10:00:00 and
59: 10:00:30 give 10:01. If there is no run within 50 × 365 days after `after` (a run exactly
60: at that limit still counts), it returns `None`. It must stay fast even then: each call
